extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars interested in Locke's theory of property and parental authority
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from John Locke's Second Treatise outlining normative principles for how private property is acquired and limited (labor-mixing, spoilage-limit, money, improvement, law/consent) and the nature and limits of parental authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slavery as a state of war; limits on master’s power
rubrics_metrics.description: “This is the perfect condition of slavery, which is nothing else, but the state of war continued, between a lawful conqueror and a captive… No body can give more power than he has himself; and he that cannot take away his own life, cannot give another power over it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slavery is characterized as the continuation of the state of war between conqueror and captive. If a compact establishes limited power and obedience, that ceases the state of war/slavery while the compact lasts. A master does not acquire absolute arbitrary power to kill at pleasure except where the person has by fault forfeited his life (e.g., a crime). A captive remains able to resist or seek death if slavery’s hardship outweighs life. (Contextual examples and qualification appear in surrounding paragraphs describing limited servitude vs. absolute despotism.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Earth given to mankind in common (starting presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: “God… has given the earth to the children of men; given it to mankind in common.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames property discussion from the premise that natural resources were initially common to all; this common grant is the background from which appropriation rules are derived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor-mixing principle: labour creates private property
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatsoever then he removes out of the state that nature hath provided, and left it in, he hath mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and thereby makes it his property.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples: gathering acorns/apples, killing game, fishing, taking ambergris — by applying one’s labour and removing resources from the natural common state one acquires property in them. No express consent of all commoners is required; labour attaches the labourer’s property to the thing. This principle underpins appropriation of both consumables and (when improved) land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriation limited by leaving 'enough, and as good' for others
rubrics_metrics.description: “…no man but he can have a right to what that is once joined to, at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation via labour is justified only when it does not deprive others of equivalent resources. This functions as a natural limit preventing harmful enclosure when it would leave others worse off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-before-spoilage limit on how much one may appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: “As much as any one can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils, so much he may by his labour fix a property in: whatever is beyond this, is more than his share, and belongs to others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may appropriate only what one can reasonably use before it perishes; hoarding perishables beyond use violates the law of nature. This spoilage-rule is the natural constraint on accumulation prior to the invention of durable money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land appropriation by cultivation/improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: “As much land as a man tills, plants, improves, cultivates, and can use the product of, so much is his property.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivating, improving, or otherwise labouring on land 'incloses' it from the common and establishes property in it. In early contexts this did not require unanimous consent of fellow-commoners, though in settled societies positive law may alter this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement increases the common stock—argument justifying enclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: “He that incloses land, and has a greater plenty of the conveniencies of life from ten acres, than he could have from an hundred left to nature, may truly be said to give ninety acres to mankind…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that labour-driven improvements make land far more productive, so enclosure (when done within limits) increases overall conveniencies of life and benefits mankind. This is used to justify private property as socially advantageous when land is improved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money (durable value) permits accumulation beyond immediate use
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thus came in the use of money, some lasting thing that men might keep without spoiling… men have agreed to a disproportionate and unequal possession of the earth, they having, by a tacit and voluntary consent, found out, a way how a man may fairly possess more land than he himself can use the product of… by putting a value on gold and silver…”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because durable minted value does not spoil, a tacit societal consent to use money enables individuals to convert perishable productive surpluses into hoardable wealth; this makes larger, unequal possessions practicable and legitimate within civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive law/compact can alter appropriation rules in civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: “In land that is common in England… no one can inclose or appropriate any part, without the consent of all his fellow-commoners; because this is left common by compact, i.e. by the law of the land… in governments, the laws regulate the right of property, and the possession of land is determined by positive constitutions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a community has by compact or law left land common, local positive law (custom, parish agreements, statutes) governs who may appropriate or enclose. The natural labour-rules are modulated by social/positive agreements and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-limits-on-hoarding: wasting/destroying common stock is wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the fruits rotted, or the venison putrified, before he could spend it, he offended against the common law of nature… he had no right, farther than his use called for any of them, and they might serve to afford him conveniencies of life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoarding beyond what one can use that results in waste or spoilage violates the natural law and effectively harms others. Trade/exchange that converts perishable goods into durable forms (or giving away) can be permissible so long as it does not waste common resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental (not merely paternal) power is joint and temporary
rubrics_metrics.description: “This may give one reason to ask, whether this might not be more properly called parental power?… she hath an equal title… Children… are not born in this full state of equality, though they are born to it. Their parents have a sort of rule and jurisdiction over them… but it is but a temporary one… age and reason as they grow up, loosen them, till at length they drop quite off, and leave a man at his own free disposal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke recommends the term 'parental power' to reflect joint authority of mother and father. Parental authority arises from obligation to preserve, nourish, and educate children until they reach reason; it is provisional and diminishes as the child matures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural equality in respect of jurisdiction (freedom from dominion)
rubrics_metrics.description: “All men by nature are equal… this equal right, that every man hath, to his natural freedom, without being subjected to the will or authority of any other man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke distinguishes kinds of equality—men may have precedency by age or virtue, but the baseline equality is an equality of natural freedom (no one has jurisdiction over another by nature). This undergirds limits on arbitrary dominion (including parental/paternal claims and slavery).
